**Operations Improvement Plan: The Certified-Flow Initiative**
*Reducing Quoted Lead Time from 14 Weeks to a Reliable 8–9 Weeks Without Quality Degradation*

---

### 1. Executive Summary

The 14-week lead time is not a quality problem; it is a **queueing and coordination problem** masked as a quality problem. Previous attempts to compress the schedule attacked the work content—forcing production to skip steps and quality to “look the other way”—which caused the warranty spike. That approach confused *inspection time* (necessary) with *inspection waiting time* (waste).

The plan below uses **Value Stream Mapping (VSM)**, **strategic decoupling inventory**, and **finite scheduling** to attack stagnation, not standards. We will protect every certified quality gate while eliminating the idle inventory and approval loops that inflate the calendar. The target is to cut quoted lead time by 40–45% within six months, with a contractual warranty risk profile lower than today’s baseline.

---

### 2. Diagnostic: Where the 14 Weeks Actually Go

Before changing anything, run a two-week time-study and VSM across five recent orders that hit the 14-week baseline. The data will almost certainly reveal the following pattern:

| Time Bucket | Share of 14 Weeks | Typical Root Cause | Owner Relationship |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Queue & Stagnation** | ~60–70% | Large transfer batches between departments; WIP piled on the floor awaiting the next operation; no WIP caps. | Production vs. Scheduling |
| **Procurement & Material Cert Wait** | ~15–20% | Long-lead castings/forgings; late engineering freeze from custom specs; mill certification delays. | Purchasing vs. Sales |
| **Inspection & Test Dwell** | ~8–12% | Batching up parts for the certified inspector; waiting for 3rd-party witness availability; test lab congestion. | Quality vs. Production |
| **Approval & Documentation** | ~3–5% | Disconnected QMS/ERP systems; manual sign-off routing; compilation of “as-built” packages after the fact. | Quality vs. IT |
| **True Value-Add Time** | ~5–8% | Actual machining, welding, assembly, and calibrated test duration. | Production |

**Key Insight:** If true value-add is <10% of the clock, we do not need to rush work; we need to **stop inventory from sitting still**. Quality gates are not consuming the weeks; the *lines of inventory waiting to hit those gates* are.

---

### 3. Strategic Framework: The "Protect the Gate, Eliminate the Queue" Doctrine

Communicate this rule to all three functions before any kaizen begins:

> *No certified inspection step will be removed or truncated. Any time saved must come from waiting time before/after the gate, from parallel processing, or from upstream prevention that makes the gate faster to clear.*

This doctrinal clarity resolves the post-traumatic standoff from the last lead-time push. Quality sees that standards are sacred; Production sees that they are not being asked to “work faster” at the expense of precision; Sales sees that shorter lead times are achievable without taking reckless promises to customers.

---

### 4. Technical Initiatives

#### A. Process & Flow Changes (Eliminate Stagnation)

| Initiative | Mechanism | Lead-Time Impact | Quality Safeguard |
|---|---|---|---|
| **WIP Caps & FIFO Lanes** | Install physical and system-level limits on inventory between operations. When an area hits its cap, upstream stops producing and fixes the flow constraint instead of burying it in inventory. | Cuts queue time 30–40% by exposing bottlenecks immediately. | Quality stations are marked as “protected resources”; WIP is allowed to accumulate 4–8 hours *in front of* inspection to prevent starving the gate, but never days. |
| **Overlapped Release** | Instead of “machine everything → then weld everything → then inspect everything,” release order-specific packages in cadences of daily flow. | Compresses calendar by 2–3 weeks via pipeline parallelism. | Each packet carries its inspection traveler so nothing enters a certified stage without pre-verified routing. |
| **Cellular Final Assembly/Test** | Move from departmental layout to a focused cell where assembly, pressure test, and final certification occur within the same physical boundary. | Eliminates transport and queue between last assembly and test. | Certified inspector is embedded in or dedicated to the cell; no batching for a roaming inspector. |

#### B. Inventory Positioning (Strategic Decoupling)

Counter-intuitively, we will **add** inventory in specific places to reduce lead time.

| Inventory Type | Location | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| **Certified Raw Material Bank** | Receiving | Hold pre-certified bar stock/plate/castings with mill certs already on file. Purchasing pulls from this bank instead of ordering to order. |
| **Post-Process Certified WIP** | After heavy machining/NDT | Parts that have cleared the longest certified stages are stored as “supermarket” inventory, then configured-to-order in final assembly. |
| **Modular Sub-Assembly** | Pre-assembly | Pre-built pump skids, control enclosures, or frame modules that have already passed structural certification. Final unit becomes “configure-to-ship” rather than full build-to-order. |

This transforms the product from a 14-week **engineer-to-order** path to an 8-week **configure-to-order** path for 70–80% of configurations.

#### C. Scheduling & Control (Finite, Not Infinite)

- **Move to Finite Scheduling**: The current 14-week quote likely assumes infinite capacity in scheduling. Switch to a rules-based, finite-capacity scheduler that loads the certified inspection/test stations first, then back-schedules machining and procurement.
- **Drum-Buffer-Rope (DBR) Implementation**: If Non-Destructive Testing (NDT) or final performance test is the constraint (it usually is), make it the *drum*. Release material into the shop based on the constraint’s capacity, not sales pressure. This prevents WIP explosions that inflate lead times.
- **Capable-to-Promise (CTP) in Sales**: Sales quotes are generated from the scheduler based on actual certified-component availability and test-cell capacity, not a static 14-week table. This stops the “say yes now, figure it out later” behavior that breaks the floor.

#### D. Supplier & Procurement Architecture

- **Extended Certified Supplier Program**: Shift material certification upstream. Suppliers with SPC data and ISO 17025-compliant labs ship with certs directly to the line; receiving inspection is reduced to a barcode scan. This cuts 1–2 weeks of incoming wait.
- **Blanket Orders + Pull Signals**: For high-volume certified components, place annual blanket POs and pull via Kanban rather than triggering 8–10 week mill lead times per order.
- **Advanced Purchase for Long-Lead Items**: Based on sales probability curves, purchasing releases forgings/castings against 60% probable orders *before* final PO. The carrying cost of 2–3 weeks of early raw stock is negligible compared to the cost of losing deals.

---

### 5. Protecting Quality Gates: The "No Compromise" Protocol

To prevent a repeat of the warranty crisis, every quality stage is protected by the following structural rules:

| Gate | Current Risk | Protective Action |
|---|---|---|
| **Incoming Material Cert** | Batches held pending full lab check. | Supplier-cert program + dock-to-line for approved vendors; random audit only. Lab reserved for new/disputed lots. |
| **In-Process Dimensional/Weld** | Parts accumulate until a roaming inspector is free. | Station a certified inspector at the cell; implement operator-led SPC with Quality audit. Inspector certifies the process, not just the part. |
| **Hydrostatic/Performance Test** | Waiting for 3rd-party witness or internal lab availability. | Pre-book witness windows based on DBR schedule (not actual completion) with a 48-hour buffer. Submit pre-read packages 24 hours before witness arrival so sign-off is same-day. |
| **Final Documentation** | As-built manuals compiled after physical shipment. | Parallel digital build: operators scan/tap work instructions in real time so the certification packet auto-compiles as the unit is built. |

**Critical Rule:** First Pass Yield (FPY) is the lead-time guardian. Every 1% improvement in FPY saves more calendar time than any scheduling trick, because rework is the most unpredictable queue of all. Production and Quality will jointly own FPY by cell, not by department.

---

### 6. Organizational Alignment: Stopping the Blame Cycle

The feud is structural: each function is optimized for a local metric that harms the system.

| Function | Current Local Metric | Systemic Dysfunction | New Shared Metric |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Sales** | Revenue; Win rate | Quotes aggressive dates to win, then pushes Production; late spec changes | **Capable-to-Promise accuracy** (how often the quoted week is the actual ship week) |
| **Production** | Output per labor hour; Utilization | Maximizes batch sizes to keep machines busy, burying inspection in WIP | **Flow time** (dock-to-stock hours) + **FPY by cell** |
| **Quality** | Defect catch rate; Audit compliance | Slows flow to inspect everything; chronically understaffed at constraint | **Certification cycle time** (clock hours at gate) + **Defects found upstream** (pre-gate prevention) |

#### Governance Structure

1. **End-to-End Value Stream Manager (VSMgr)**
   - Appoint a senior leader with authority over Production, Quality, and Sales coordination for this product line. They own the 8–9 week promise to the customer, not the functional VPs.

2. **Weekly Time-Loss Huddle**
   - 30-minute stand-up with Production, Quality, Sales, and Scheduling.
   - Review the five orders closest to ship date.
   - Use **object-code root cause only**: *Material Wait, Inspection Wait, Rework, Spec Change, or Capacity Shortage*. No blame; the code names the system failure.

3. **Joint Warranty Watch**
   - Any proposed change that touches a certified stage requires a joint sign-off by the three functional heads and a 30/60/90-day warranty readout plan. This institutionalizes the trauma from the prior spike into a governance gate.

4. **Visual Control Room**
   - Large-screen value stream map showing live WIP by stage, inspector schedule, and constraint status. When all three functions see the same data, argument turns into problem-solving.

---

### 7. Implementation Roadmap

| Phase | Duration | Actions | Target Outcome |
|---|---|---|---|
| **I: Baseline** | Weeks 1–4 | Run VSM/time study on five orders; map true constraint; install WIP caps on two pilot cells; launch supplier-cert pilot with top two vendors. | Identify exact hour-by-hour time loss; prove WIP-cap concept. |
| **II: Quick Wins** | Weeks 5–12 | Deploy finite scheduling/CTP in Sales; add second shift or dedicated inspector to the NDT/Test constraint; implement digital as-built documentation; standardize top 20% configurations to modular BOMs. | Quoted lead time drops to 10–11 weeks; FNY holds or improves. |
| **III: Structural Flow** | Weeks 13–26 | Scale modular sub-assembly inventory; roll out certified raw-material bank; extend supplier-cert program to 80% of spend; convert final assembly to cellular layout. | Quoted lead time hits 8–9 weeks on standard configs; 3rd-party witness scheduling becomes routine. |
| **IV: Systematize** | Weeks 27–52 | Refine DBR scheduling across full shop; train all operators in SPC; lock in metrics; monthly audit of quality gate dwell time. | New operating rhythm is the default; warranty claims tracked in weekly huddle with closed-loop feedback. |

---

### 8. Metrics & Risk Controls

Track these weekly to ensure speed does not cannibalize quality:

| Metric | Baseline | Target | Owner |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Quoted Customer Lead Time** | 14 weeks | 8–9 weeks (std); 11 weeks (custom) | Sales / VSMgr |
| **Quality Gate Dwell Time** | Unmeasured | <8 hours per stage (except 3rd-party witness) | Quality / VSMgr |
| **First Pass Yield (by cell)** | Current average | Improve 3% over baseline | Production + Quality |
| **Warranty defect rate (30/60/90-day)** | Baseline from last 24 months | Lower than baseline | Quality |
| **CTP Accuracy** | <50% (estimated) | >85% | Sales |
| **WIP Inventory Turns** | Low | Increase 40% | Production |

**Risk Mitigation:**
- **Pilot Containment:** Run Phase II on one product family or one geographic sales region to prove the warranty profile is neutral or positive before universal rollout.
- **No Gate Removal Rule:** Any executive who proposes eliminating a certified step to “go faster” must present a revised FMEA and obtain Quality VP sign-off.
- **Capacity Investment:** If the constraint is truly inspection, we may need to hire or train one to two additional certified inspectors. This is a planned investment, not a failure. It pays for itself with three retained deals.

---

### Bottom Line

You do not have a 14-week manufacturing problem. You have a **14-week logistics-and-queueing problem** that your organization misinterprets as a quality-vs.-speed tradeoff. By capping WIP, decoupling long certified cycles with strategic inventory, scheduling to the constraint, and embedding quality into cells rather than letting it become a departmental bottleneck, you can deliver a substantially faster quote to customers while operating a *tighter* quality system than you have today. The alignment of the three feuding functions happens not through compromise, but through a shared visual system where the enemy is the queue, not each other.
